scheduling_implication: Orlistat can reduce the absorption or effect of amiodarone. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

mechanism_type: soy protein binding / reduced levothyroxine absorption
evidence_text: The Synthroid label states that soybean flour (and soybean-based infant formula) may bind and decrease levothyroxine absorption, and advises 4 h separation from interfering agents. Case reports describe higher levothyroxine dose requirements with soy protein supplements and soy formula in congenital hypothyroidism. No controlled PK magnitude is available.
scheduling_implication: Soy foods can reduce the absorption or effect of thyroid hormone (levothyroxine). Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: In Benvenga et al. 2008 (Thyroid), espresso coffee taken with or shortly after levothyroxine tablets reduced T4 absorption in volunteers and in patients with poor control. Absorption normalized when coffee was delayed by at least 60 min. The study was small and the effect is formulation-dependent (liquid/softgel forms are less affected).
evidence_scope: small human absorption study + case series
scheduling_implication: Coffee can reduce the absorption or effect of thyroid hormone (levothyroxine). Take them at least 1 hour apart.

mechanism_type: gastric pH rise reducing tablet levothyroxine dissolution
evidence_text: The Synthroid label states that gastric acidity is essential for levothyroxine absorption and that PPIs may cause hypochlorhydria and reduce absorption. In Centanni et al. 2006 (NEJM), patients with H. pylori/atrophic gastritis and patients on omeprazole needed higher T4 doses to reach target TSH. Other studies show smaller or inconsistent TSH changes, and liquid formulations are largely unaffected.
scheduling_implication: Proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) can lower the levels or effect of thyroid hormone (levothyroxine) throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether thyroid hormone (levothyroxine) needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: The Synthroid label states that dietary fiber may bind and decrease levothyroxine absorption. Liel et al. 1996 (JCEM) found that a fiber-enriched diet raised levothyroxine requirements in hypothyroid adults. A study of pharmacological fiber supplements (psyllium) found little effect, so the size of the effect depends on fiber type.
scheduling_implication: Dietary fiber can reduce the absorption or effect of thyroid hormone (levothyroxine). Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: The only primary data is a small volunteer study (Etman 1995, Drug Dev Ind Pharm) reporting reduced carbamazepine bioavailability with psyllium. It is not indexed in PubMed and could not be retrieved to confirm the magnitude. Secondary monographs list fiber as possibly decreasing carbamazepine absorption.
scheduling_implication: Psyllium can reduce the absorption or effect of carbamazepine. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: The Dilantin label lists folic acid among agents that may decrease phenytoin serum levels and counsels that vitamins such as folic acid can alter phenytoin levels. Clinical reports and PK studies show folic acid supplementation lowers phenytoin concentrations, most markedly in folate-deficient patients, and can cause loss of seizure control.
scheduling_implication: Folic acid can lower the levels or effect of phenytoin throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether phenytoin needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: Hansson & Sillanpää (1976 Lancet letter) reported that pyridoxine 200 mg/day for 4 weeks lowered serum phenytoin (about 50% in some patients) and phenobarbitone in epileptic patients. This is a single small uncontrolled report; the Dilantin label does not list pyridoxine. It is relevant only at high doses.
scheduling_implication: Vitamin B6 can lower the levels or effect of phenytoin throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether phenytoin needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: The Dilantin label lists calcium carbonate and antacids as possibly affecting phenytoin absorption and says phenytoin and antacids should not be taken at the same time of day. Small single-dose human studies of calcium and antacids gave inconsistent, generally modest reductions in phenytoin bioavailability.
evidence_scope: FDA label + small human PK studies
scheduling_implication: Calcium carbonate can reduce the absorption or effect of phenytoin. Take them at least 2 hours apart.

evidence_text: The ketoconazole tablet label reports that after omeprazole pretreatment, fasted bioavailability of a single 200 mg dose fell to 17% of control. Taking it with non-diet cola restored bioavailability to 65%. The label lists PPIs as acid suppressors that impair ketoconazole absorption.
scheduling_implication: Proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) can lower the levels or effect of ketoconazole throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether ketoconazole needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: The ketoconazole label lists H2-receptor antagonists as acid secretion suppressors that impair absorption and recommends an acidic beverage with co-treatment. Lelawongs et al. 1988 showed that drug-induced gastric hypoacidity (cimetidine plus sodium bicarbonate) markedly reduced ketoconazole absorption, which was restored by acidification.
scheduling_implication: H2 blockers (e.g., famotidine) can lower the levels or effect of ketoconazole throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether ketoconazole needs monitoring or a dose change.

from_mechanism_name: Antacid / gastric-pH-raising mineral salt (Ca carbonate, Mg/Al hydroxide, Na bicarbonate)
evidence_text: The ketoconazole tablet label instructs that acid-neutralizing medicines (e.g., aluminum hydroxide) be given at least 1 h before or 2 h after ketoconazole, because dissolution and absorption need gastric acid.
scheduling_implication: Antacids can reduce the absorption or effect of ketoconazole. Take ketoconazole at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after antacids.

evidence_text: In Jaruratanasirikul & Sriwiriyajan 1998, omeprazole 40 mg/day for 14 days in healthy volunteers reduced itraconazole capsule AUC by about 64% and Cmax by about 66%. The Sporanox label states that capsule absorption is reduced with gastric acid secretion suppressors. Oral solution and SUBA formulations are much less affected.
scheduling_implication: Proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) can lower the levels or effect of itraconazole throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether itraconazole needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: The Sporanox label notes reduced itraconazole capsule absorption with acid suppressors; in a fasted study, cola taken after ranitidine pretreatment brought absorption back to that of capsules alone. Lange et al. 1997 and Lim et al. 1993 showed lower itraconazole absorption under H2-blocker-induced hypochlorhydria.
evidence_scope: FDA label + small human PK studies
scheduling_implication: H2 blockers (e.g., famotidine) can lower the levels or effect of itraconazole throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether itraconazole needs monitoring or a dose change.

from_mechanism_name: Antacid / gastric-pH-raising mineral salt (Ca carbonate, Mg/Al hydroxide, Na bicarbonate)
evidence_text: The current Sporanox capsule label says to give acid-neutralizing medicines (e.g., aluminum hydroxide) at least 2 h before or 2 h after itraconazole capsules. A healthy-volunteer study found that an antacid suspension significantly reduced oral itraconazole bioavailability.
scheduling_implication: Antacids can reduce the absorption or effect of itraconazole. Take itraconazole at least 2 hours before or 2 hours after antacids.

evidence_text: In O'Connell et al. 2005 (Am J Med, randomized crossover, women aged 65 and over), omeprazole 20 mg for 7 days significantly reduced fractional absorption of calcium carbonate taken fasting. Hansen et al. 2010 found no reduction with 30 days of omeprazole when calcium was taken with meals. NIH ODS notes that carbonate solubility falls with low stomach acid unless it is taken with a meal; citrate is less acid-dependent.
evidence_scope: human RCT crossover (fasting) + conflicting fed-state RCT
scheduling_implication: Proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) can lower the levels or effect of calcium carbonate throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether calcium carbonate needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: Hutchinson et al. 2007 (Gut) showed that PPIs suppressed absorption of dietary non-heme iron from a test meal and reduced maintenance phlebotomy needs in hereditary hemochromatosis. NIH ODS states that PPIs can reduce iron absorption and that iron-deficient patients on PPIs may respond suboptimally to iron supplements, though long-term use does not cause depletion in people with normal stores.
scheduling_implication: Proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) can lower the levels or effect of iron throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether iron needs monitoring or a dose change.

mechanism_type: reduced release of protein-bound B12 (crystalline supplemental B12 much less affected)
evidence_text: Saltzman et al. 1994 showed that omeprazole-induced hypochlorhydria reduced absorption of protein-bound (food) vitamin B12. NIH ODS states that acid suppressors interfere with B12 absorption from food, while supplemental B12 is already free and does not need acid release. The effect on crystalline supplement B12 is therefore expected to be small.
scheduling_implication: Long-term PPI use mainly reduces absorption of vitamin B12 from food; B12 supplements are much less affected. Consider periodic B12 checks with long-term PPI use.

evidence_text: In 12 healthy volunteers given St John's wort 300 mg three times daily for 14 days, alprazolam AUC fell about 2-fold and clearance roughly doubled, with elimination half-life shortened from 12.4 h to 6.0 h (all P<0.001). The effect is enzyme induction, so it persists for days after the herb is stopped and cannot be managed by hour-level dose separation.
scheduling_implication: St John's wort can lower the levels or effect of alprazolam throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether alprazolam needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: In 16 healthy women on a low-dose oral contraceptive, St John's wort 300 mg three times daily for two cycles reduced contraceptive steroid exposure by only 13-15%, but increased breakthrough bleeding, follicle growth and probable ovulation. The PK reduction is small while the pharmacodynamic consequence (loss of ovulation suppression) is clinically important.
evidence_scope: human sequential crossover with ovarian activity endpoints, n=16 (Contraception 2005)
scheduling_implication: St John's wort can lower the levels or effect of oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol) throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol) needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: Johne et al. (J Clin Psychopharmacol 2002) reported decreased plasma levels of amitriptyline and its metabolites in depressed patients comedicated with a St John's wort extract, consistent with CYP/P-gp induction. The exact AUC percentages could not be re-confirmed from the abstract page (NCBI access was blocked during this review), so the magnitude rests on the reported direction only.
evidence_scope: human comedication PK study in depressed patients (title/record confirmed, abstract numbers unverified)
scheduling_implication: St John's wort can lower the levels or effect of amitriptyline throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether amitriptyline needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: Wang et al. (2004) showed St John's wort induces both CYP3A4-catalysed sulfoxidation and CYP2C19-dependent hydroxylation of omeprazole in healthy subjects, lowering omeprazole plasma exposure across CYP2C19 genotype groups. The abstract's exact AUC reduction could not be retrieved during this review, so a >50% ('major') effect is not demonstrated by confirmed text.
evidence_scope: human PK study stratified by CYP2C19 genotype (record confirmed, numbers unverified)
scheduling_implication: St John's wort can lower the levels or effect of omeprazole throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether omeprazole needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: In 14 healthy men, two weeks of St John's wort reduced zolpidem AUC by about 30% (380 to 265 ng.h/mL, P=0.001) and Cmax by about 34%, with CL/F increased ~48%. The study was open-label and non-randomised with wide inter-subject variability (AUC rose slightly in 3 of 14 subjects).
evidence_scope: human PK open-label, n=14 (J Clin Pharm Ther 2011)
scheduling_implication: St John's wort can lower the levels or effect of zolpidem throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether zolpidem needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: St John's wort induces intestinal P-glycoprotein/MDR1 and intestinal and hepatic CYP3A4 on repeated dosing, which would lower exposure to the P-gp substrate fexofenadine; however the dedicated single-dose fexofenadine study (Wang et al., Clin Pharmacol Ther 2002) found the opposite acute direction, so acute and chronic effects conflict. Net chronic effect on fexofenadine is small and not firmly established.
evidence_scope: human mechanistic induction study plus conflicting single-dose fexofenadine PK study
scheduling_implication: St John's wort can lower the levels or effect of fexofenadine throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether fexofenadine needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: In healthy adults given oral midazolam 2.5 mg, goldenseal raised midazolam AUC with geometric mean ratios of 1.39 (90% CI 1.30-1.48) after 1 g three times daily for 6 days (n=16) and 1.57 (1.39-1.77) after a single 3 g dose (n=8); Cmax ratios were 1.31 and 1.40. PBPK work attributes this mainly to intestinal CYP3A inhibition, with no predicted change for IV midazolam.
evidence_scope: human PK, n=16 chronic / n=8 acute (J Pharmacol Exp Ther 2023, PMID 37541764), plus Gurley 2005 phenotype study
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: goldenseal can raise midazolam levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: In 16 healthy volunteers, goldenseal decreased metformin AUC0-inf with a geometric mean ratio of 0.77 (90% CI 0.71-0.83), with no change in half-life or renal clearance, pointing to reduced intestinal absorption rather than altered renal transport. The authors note this could unfavourably affect glucose control.
evidence_scope: human probe-cocktail PK, n=16 (Clin Pharmacol Ther 2021, PMID 33174626)
scheduling_implication: Goldenseal can lower the levels or effect of metformin throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether metformin needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: In renal transplant recipients, berberine 0.2 g three times daily raised cyclosporine A exposure: in a 6-patient PK study AUC and Css rose 34.5%, Cmin rose 88.3% and CL/F fell 40.4%, and in a controlled comparison (52 vs 52 patients, 3 months) berberine-treated trough levels were ~29% higher than controls. Evidence is from a single centre in transplant patients rather than a formal crossover in healthy subjects.
evidence_scope: human PK n=6 plus controlled clinical comparison n=104 (Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2005)
scheduling_implication: Avoid this combination unless a clinician approves: berberine can raise cyclosporine levels and increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: In healthy male subjects given berberine 300 mg three times daily for 2 weeks, midazolam Cmax rose 38% and AUC(0-inf) rose 40%, with oral clearance down 27% and the midazolam/1'-hydroxymidazolam ratio up 59%, indicating CYP3A4 inhibition. Sample size is not stated in the abstract.
evidence_scope: human probe-drug PK vs placebo (Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2012)
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: berberine can raise midazolam levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

mechanism_type: CYP2C9 inhibition reducing active E-3174 formation
evidence_text: In the same berberine probe study (300 mg three times daily, 2 weeks), the losartan/E-3174 metabolic ratio doubled (P<0.01), indicating meaningful CYP2C9 inhibition and reduced formation of losartan's active metabolite. The study measured metabolic ratios rather than clinical blood-pressure effect.
evidence_scope: human probe-drug PK, metabolic ratio endpoint (Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2012)
scheduling_implication: Berberine can lower the levels or effect of losartan throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether losartan needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: Gurley et al. assessed goldenseal, kava kava, black cohosh and valerian against CYP1A2, 2D6, 2E1 and 3A4/5 probes in healthy volunteers and identified kava as an in vivo inhibitor of CYP2E1 (6-hydroxychlorzoxazone/chlorzoxazone ratio). The exact percentage inhibition could not be re-confirmed during this review, and chlorzoxazone is a probe rather than a commonly co-taken drug.
evidence_scope: human CYP phenotype study with chlorzoxazone probe (Clin Pharmacol Ther 2005, record confirmed; magnitude unverified)
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: kava can raise chlorzoxazone levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: In elderly subjects, garlic oil supplementation significantly inhibited CYP2E1 activity by about 22% (6-OH-chlorzoxazone/chlorzoxazone ratio 0.423 to 0.331, P=0.005) while CYP3A4 (midazolam ratio) was unchanged. The effect is modest and demonstrated with a probe substrate.
evidence_scope: human CYP phenotype study in the elderly, chlorzoxazone probe (Drugs Aging 2005, PMID 15974642)
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: garlic oil can raise chlorzoxazone levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

mechanism_type: CYP2C9 inhibition reducing active E-3174 formation
evidence_text: In 12 healthy Chinese men (6 CYP2C9*1/*1, 6 CYP2C9*1/*3), 14 days of silymarin significantly increased losartan AUC in *1/*1 subjects and significantly decreased the AUC of the active metabolite E-3174 in both genotype groups. Effect sizes are small and genotype-dependent, and no blood-pressure outcome was measured.
evidence_scope: human PK crossover by CYP2C9 genotype, n=12 (Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2009)
scheduling_implication: Silymarin can lower the levels or effect of losartan throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether losartan needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: In 12 healthy volunteers, silymarin 140 mg/day for 9 days increased the clearance of metronidazole by 29.5% and of hydroxy-metronidazole by 31.9%, with corresponding decreases in half-life, Cmax and AUC(0-48) and reduced 48-h urinary excretion. Single small study with an induction (not inhibition) mechanism proposed.
scheduling_implication: Silymarin can lower the levels or effect of metronidazole throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether metronidazole needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: Yuan et al. reported in a randomised controlled trial that American ginseng reduced warfarin's anticoagulant effect in healthy subjects (lower INR and warfarin exposure versus placebo). This is a randomised human trial with a clinical pharmacodynamic endpoint, which supports high confidence for the direction.
evidence_scope: randomised controlled trial in healthy subjects (Ann Intern Med 2004)
scheduling_implication: American ginseng can lower the levels or effect of warfarin throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether warfarin needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: Yin et al. (Pharmacogenetics 2004) reported that Ginkgo biloba extract induces CYP2C19-mediated hydroxylation of omeprazole in healthy subjects, lowering omeprazole exposure with the effect depending on CYP2C19 genotype. A single genotype-stratified study; magnitudes were not re-confirmed here.
evidence_scope: human PK study stratified by CYP2C19 genotype (record confirmed)
scheduling_implication: Ginkgo can lower the levels or effect of omeprazole throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether omeprazole needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: The fexofenadine (ALLEGRA) label states that fruit juices such as grapefruit, orange and apple may reduce the bioavailability and exposure of fexofenadine, with bioavailability reduced by 36% in pooled population-PK and bioequivalence data, and recommends taking the tablets with water. The label adds that the clinical significance of the observation is unknown; the mechanism is transient intestinal OATP inhibition, so separating intake helps.
scheduling_implication: Grapefruit can reduce the absorption or effect of fexofenadine. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: The Tegretol (carbamazepine) label lists grapefruit juice among CYP3A4 inhibitors that may raise carbamazepine plasma levels, and the Medication Guide tells patients to report grapefruit use. The specific human study magnitude (Garg 1998) could not be re-confirmed during this review, so confidence stays medium.
evidence_scope: FDA label (CYP3A4 inhibitor list naming grapefruit juice)
scheduling_implication: Avoid this combination unless a clinician approves: grapefruit can raise carbamazepine levels and increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: Quetiapine (Seroquel) product information instructs patients not to drink grapefruit juice while taking the drug because it can affect how the medicine works, consistent with CYP3A inhibition raising quetiapine exposure. The statement is qualitative, with no quantified AUC change for grapefruit specifically.
evidence_scope: regulatory product information (HPRA Seroquel package leaflet)
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: grapefruit can raise quetiapine levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: Bano et al. (1991) gave piperine 20 mg daily for 7 days to healthy volunteers (6 per group, crossover) and found a single 40 mg propranolol dose reached peak concentration earlier with higher Cmax and higher AUC. The abstract reports direction only, with no numeric AUC/Cmax values, and the sample is very small.
evidence_scope: human PK crossover, n=6 (Eur J Clin Pharmacol 1991)
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: piperine can raise propranolol levels, which may increase its side effects.

evidence_text: In the same study, piperine 20 mg daily for 7 days raised the Cmax and AUC of a single 150 mg theophylline dose and prolonged its elimination half-life in healthy volunteers (6 per group). Direction only, no numeric magnitudes, n=6, and theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index so even an unquantified rise matters clinically.
evidence_scope: human PK crossover, n=6 (Eur J Clin Pharmacol 1991)
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: piperine can raise theophylline levels, which may increase its side effects.

evidence_text: Kusuhara et al. (Br J Pharmacol 2012) used sulphasalazine as a BCRP probe in healthy subjects and showed that oral curcumin increases sulphasalazine plasma exposure, establishing curcumin as an in vivo BCRP inhibitor. The exact fold-change could not be re-confirmed during this review; the mechanism is intestinal and competitive, so hour-level separation is plausible mitigation.
evidence_scope: human probe-substrate PK study (record confirmed, PMID 22300367; magnitude unverified)
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: curcumin can raise sulfasalazine levels, which may increase its side effects.

evidence_text: In 12 healthy male volunteers, Schisandra sphenanthera extract (3 capsules twice daily for 7 days) increased midazolam AUC by a mean 119.4% (95% CI 83.9-155.0) and Cmax by 85.6%, with CL/F reduced 52.1% and no change in half-life. Single-centre study in one ethnic group with a non-standardised extract.
evidence_scope: human PK, n=12 (Br J Clin Pharmacol 2009)
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: schisandra can raise midazolam levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: Gorski et al. (Clin Pharmacol Ther 2004) studied Echinacea purpurea root on CYP activity in vivo in healthy volunteers using caffeine, tolbutamide, dextromethorphan and midazolam probes and reported modest CYP1A2 inhibition (reduced caffeine clearance) alongside opposing intestinal and hepatic CYP3A effects. The caffeine magnitude could not be re-confirmed during this review and is generally reported as small.
evidence_scope: human probe-cocktail PK study (record confirmed, PMID 14749695; magnitude unverified)
scheduling_implication: Echinacea supports the use or levels of caffeine over time; no special timing is needed.

evidence_text: The ciprofloxacin label states that concomitant use with caffeine or other xanthine derivatives may lead to reduced clearance of caffeine and prolongation of its serum half-life, and that ciprofloxacin inhibits the formation of paraxanthine after caffeine administration; use with caution and monitor for xanthine toxicity. No numeric fold-change is given in the label.
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: ciprofloxacin can raise caffeine levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: Cimetidine is named on the duloxetine label as a drug that inhibits CYP1A2 metabolism, the pathway responsible for caffeine clearance, and caffeine-specific studies (Broughton & Rogers 1981; May 1982) report decreased systemic caffeine clearance with cimetidine. Those primary caffeine papers could not be opened during this review (NCBI access blocked), so the magnitude is unverified here.
evidence_scope: FDA label CYP1A2 inhibitor statement plus cited (unretrieved) human caffeine PK studies
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: cimetidine can raise caffeine levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

mechanism_type: CYP1A2 inhibition by oral contraceptive steroids
evidence_text: Abernethy & Todd showed impairment of caffeine clearance with chronic use of low-dose oestrogen-containing oral contraceptives in human subjects, consistent with CYP1A2 inhibition by contraceptive steroids. The effect builds with chronic steroid dosing, so it is a whole-day exposure shift rather than something hour-level separation can avoid.
evidence_scope: human PK comparison, OC users vs controls (Eur J Clin Pharmacol 1985)
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol) can raise caffeine levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: Viloxazine ER is labelled a strong CYP1A2 inhibitor and is contraindicated with sensitive CYP1A2 substrates or CYP1A2 substrates with a narrow therapeutic range. In a dedicated clinical study, viloxazine ER raised caffeine AUCt to 436% of control (90% CI 399-477), i.e. roughly a 4.4- to 5.8-fold increase in exposure, while Cmax was essentially unchanged (99%).
evidence_scope: FDA label contraindication plus human PK interaction study (Clin Drug Investig 2024)
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: viloxazine can raise caffeine levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: The Circadin (prolonged-release melatonin) SmPC states that fluvoxamine increases melatonin levels 17-fold in AUC and 12-fold in serum Cmax by inhibiting CYP1A2 and CYP2C19, and that the combination should be avoided. Fluvoxamine's long half-life and enzyme inhibition make this a whole-day effect.
evidence_scope: EMA SmPC section 4.5 (plus Hartter 2000 human PK)
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: fluvoxamine can raise melatonin levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: In 12 healthy subjects (6 smokers, 6 non-smokers), caffeine 3 x 200 mg coadministered with 6 mg melatonin increased melatonin Cmax by an average 142% and AUC by 120%, with a stronger effect in non-smokers. Mechanism is competitive CYP1A2 metabolism, so the interaction tracks caffeine's own disposition and separating intake reduces overlap.
evidence_scope: human PK crossover, n=12 (Br J Clin Pharmacol 2003)
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: caffeine can raise melatonin levels, which may increase its side effects.

evidence_text: Melatonin AUC and Cmax were 4- to 5-fold higher in oral contraceptive users than in non-users (n=29, P<0.0001), and the Circadin SmPC warns that oestrogens (contraceptives or HRT) increase melatonin levels by inhibiting CYP1A1/CYP1A2. Both a human study and an authoritative label statement support the rule.
evidence_scope: human PK comparison n=29 (Eur J Clin Pharmacol 2008) plus EMA SmPC
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol) can raise melatonin levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: The Valdoxan (agomelatine) SmPC contraindicates concomitant use of potent CYP1A2 inhibitors and states that fluvoxamine markedly inhibits agomelatine metabolism, resulting in a 60-fold (range 12-412) increase in agomelatine exposure. This is an absolute label contraindication, not a timing problem.
scheduling_implication: Avoid this combination unless a clinician approves: fluvoxamine can raise agomelatine levels and increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: The Valdoxan SmPC section 4.3 contraindicates concomitant use of potent CYP1A2 inhibitors and names ciprofloxacin explicitly alongside fluvoxamine. The contraindication is categorical, so no separation interval makes the combination acceptable.
evidence_scope: EMA SmPC section 4.3 (explicit contraindication naming ciprofloxacin)
scheduling_implication: Avoid this combination unless a clinician approves: ciprofloxacin can raise agomelatine levels and increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: The CLOZARIL label directs reducing the clozapine dose to one-third of the original dose when coadministered with strong CYP1A2 inhibitors including fluvoxamine. In 16 patients with schizophrenia at clozapine steady state, 14 days of fluvoxamine raised mean trough clozapine and metabolite concentrations about three-fold.
evidence_scope: FDA label section 7.1 dosing instruction plus label PK study n=16
scheduling_implication: Avoid this combination unless a clinician approves: fluvoxamine can raise clozapine levels and increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: The CLOZARIL label lists ciprofloxacin among the strong CYP1A2 inhibitors for which the clozapine dose must be reduced to one-third of the original dose, with the dose restored when the inhibitor is stopped. A label-mandated two-thirds dose reduction corresponds to a major exposure change.
evidence_scope: FDA label section 7.1 (strong CYP1A2 inhibitor dosing instruction)
scheduling_implication: Avoid this combination unless a clinician approves: ciprofloxacin can raise clozapine levels and increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: The fluvoxamine maleate label states that theophylline clearance was decreased approximately 3-fold with fluvoxamine and that the theophylline dose should be reduced to one-third of the usual daily maintenance dose. Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index, so this is a major whole-day exposure change.
scheduling_implication: Avoid this combination unless a clinician approves: fluvoxamine can raise theophylline levels and increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: The ciprofloxacin label carries a prominent warning that serious and fatal reactions have been reported with concurrent ciprofloxacin and theophylline, attributed to elevated serum theophylline concentrations and prolonged elimination half-life; current labelling lists theophylline under 'avoid use'. If coadministration is unavoidable, theophylline levels must be monitored and the dose adjusted.
evidence_scope: FDA label warning and drug-interaction table
scheduling_implication: Avoid this combination unless a clinician approves: ciprofloxacin can raise theophylline levels and increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: The CYMBALTA label states that when duloxetine 60 mg was coadministered with fluvoxamine 100 mg, duloxetine AUC increased approximately 6-fold, Cmax about 2.5-fold and half-life about 3-fold, and that coadministration with potent CYP1A2 inhibitors should be avoided. The ~6-fold AUC rise plus a tripled half-life makes this a whole-day effect.
scheduling_implication: Avoid this combination unless a clinician approves: fluvoxamine can raise duloxetine levels and increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: The ciprofloxacin label lists duloxetine under 'avoid use' and quantifies a five-fold increase in duloxetine exposure, advising monitoring for duloxetine toxicity if coadministration is unavoidable; the CYMBALTA label independently names ciprofloxacin and enoxacin as CYP1A2 inhibitors to avoid. Two concordant labels with a quantified five-fold exposure increase.
evidence_scope: FDA labels (Cipro interaction table; Cymbalta sections 5.12/7.1)
scheduling_implication: Avoid this combination unless a clinician approves: ciprofloxacin can raise duloxetine levels and increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: The CLOZARIL label lists caffeine (with oral contraceptives) as an example of a moderate or weak CYP1A2 inhibitor, advising close monitoring and consideration of a clozapine dose reduction. Unlike the strong inhibitors, no fixed dose fraction is specified, consistent with a moderate rather than major effect.
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: caffeine can raise clozapine levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: The STRATTERA label reports that coadministration of fluoxetine produced 6- to 8-fold increases in steady-state atomoxetine AUC in subjects who are not CYP2D6 poor metabolisers, with Css,max about 3- to 4-fold greater than atomoxetine alone. Fluoxetine's very long half-life makes this a whole-day effect that persists for weeks after stopping.
evidence_scope: FDA label section 12.3 PK interaction data
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: fluoxetine can raise atomoxetine levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: The STRATTERA label reports that paroxetine coadministration resulted in 6.5-fold higher steady-state atomoxetine AUC in subjects who are not CYP2D6 poor metabolisers, with Css,max about 3- to 4-fold greater than atomoxetine alone. Strong CYP2D6 inhibition is sustained across the dosing interval.
evidence_scope: FDA label section 12.3 PK interaction data
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: paroxetine can raise atomoxetine levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: In a two-period healthy-volunteer study, 7 days of bupropion pretreatment plus bupropion 300 mg raised single-dose atomoxetine 25 mg AUC(0-inf) from about 1580 to 8060 ng.h/mL (roughly a 5.1-fold increase) and Cmax from 226 to 386 ng/mL. Bupropion is not named on the STRATTERA label, and the published sample size is not stated in the abstract, so confidence stays medium.
evidence_scope: human PK two-period study (J Pharm Pharm Sci 2016, DOI 10.18433/J3H03R)
scheduling_implication: Use with caution: bupropion can raise atomoxetine levels, which may increase its side effects. Spacing the doses does not help.

evidence_text: Combined oral contraceptives containing ethinyl estradiol induce lamotrigine glucuronidation and lower lamotrigine levels by roughly 50%; levels rise again during the pill-free week. The lamotrigine label requires dose adjustment when starting or stopping estrogen-containing contraceptives.
scheduling_implication: Oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol) can lower the levels or effect of lamotrigine throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether lamotrigine needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: Carbamazepine induces UGT glucuronidation and roughly halves lamotrigine exposure (half-life falls from about 26 h to about 13 h); the label gives a separate dosing schedule for patients on enzyme-inducing antiepileptics.
scheduling_implication: Carbamazepine can lower the levels or effect of lamotrigine throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether lamotrigine needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: Phenytoin induces UGT glucuronidation and roughly halves lamotrigine exposure; the label gives a separate dosing schedule for patients on enzyme-inducing antiepileptics.
scheduling_implication: Phenytoin can lower the levels or effect of lamotrigine throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether lamotrigine needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: Phenobarbital (and primidone) induce UGT glucuronidation and roughly halve lamotrigine exposure; the label gives a separate dosing schedule for patients on enzyme-inducing antiepileptics.
scheduling_implication: Phenobarbital can lower the levels or effect of lamotrigine throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether lamotrigine needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: Rifampin induces glucuronidation and lowered lamotrigine exposure by about 40-45% in healthy volunteers; the label recommends the enzyme-inducer dosing schedule.
scheduling_implication: Rifampin can lower the levels or effect of lamotrigine throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether lamotrigine needs monitoring or a dose change.

mechanism_type: antibacterial killing of co-administered live bacteria
evidence_text: Antibiotics can kill live bacterial probiotics taken at the same time. Probiotic guidance commonly advises taking bacterial probiotics at least 2 hours apart from antibiotic doses; spore-forming Bacillus strains and the yeast S. boulardii are much less affected.
evidence_scope: NIH ODS fact sheet (probiotics); probiotic labeling
scheduling_implication: Antibiotics can kill live bacterial probiotics taken at the same time. Take the probiotic at least 2 hours apart from the antibiotic (spore-forming Bacillus strains and S. boulardii are less affected).

mechanism_type: antifungal killing of live yeast probiotic
evidence_text: Saccharomyces boulardii is a live yeast and is killed by systemic antifungal drugs; product labeling (e.g., Florastor) advises against taking it together with antifungals.
scheduling_implication: Azole antifungals can kill the probiotic yeast Saccharomyces boulardii for as long as the antifungal is being taken; spacing doses does not help, so expect reduced benefit during antifungal treatment.

mechanism_type: CYP induction accelerating vitamin D catabolism
evidence_text: Enzyme-inducing antiepileptics (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) speed up hepatic breakdown of vitamin D; long-term users have lower 25(OH)D levels and more bone loss/osteomalacia.
evidence_scope: NIH ODS fact sheet (vitamin D); clinical reviews
scheduling_implication: Enzyme-inducing antiepileptics (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) can lower the levels or effect of vitamin D3 throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether vitamin D3 needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: Long-term use of enzyme-inducing antiepileptics (especially phenytoin, phenobarbital and carbamazepine) is associated with low serum and red-cell folate in a substantial share of patients.
evidence_scope: NIH ODS fact sheet (folate); clinical studies
scheduling_implication: Enzyme-inducing antiepileptics (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) can lower the levels or effect of folic acid throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether folic acid needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: Long-term use of enzyme-inducing antiepileptics is associated with low folate status; the depletion applies to all folate forms, including methylfolate.
evidence_scope: NIH ODS fact sheet (folate); clinical studies
scheduling_implication: Enzyme-inducing antiepileptics (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) can lower the levels or effect of methylfolate (5-MTHF) throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether methylfolate (5-MTHF) needs monitoring or a dose change.

evidence_text: Carbamazepine, phenytoin and phenobarbital lower biotin status, likely by speeding biotin breakdown and inhibiting its intestinal uptake; long-term users show reduced plasma biotin and raised markers of biotin deficiency.
evidence_scope: NIH ODS fact sheet (biotin); human studies (Krause 1982, Mock 1997)
scheduling_implication: Enzyme-inducing antiepileptics (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) can lower the levels or effect of biotin throughout the day, so spacing the doses does not help. If both are used regularly, ask a clinician whether biotin needs monitoring or a dose change.

mechanism_type: calcium inhibition of non-heme and heme iron absorption
evidence_text: Calcium (about 300-600 mg from supplements or dairy) taken with a meal or iron dose reduced both non-heme and heme iron absorption by roughly 30-60% in single-meal studies; the effect is smaller over longer periods.
evidence_scope: human absorption studies (Hallberg 1991); NIH ODS fact sheet
scheduling_implication: Calcium can reduce the absorption or effect of iron. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

mechanism_type: ascorbate reduction/chelation enhancing non-heme iron absorption
evidence_text: Vitamin C reduces ferric to ferrous iron and keeps it soluble, increasing non-heme iron absorption about 2-fold or more when taken in the same meal or dose.
evidence_scope: human absorption studies; NIH ODS fact sheet
scheduling_implication: Taking vitamin C together with iron (within about 1 hour) can help iron work better.

evidence_text: Supplemental iron taken on an empty stomach together with zinc (iron:zinc ratio of 2:1 or higher) reduces zinc absorption; the effect largely disappears when both are taken with food.
evidence_scope: human absorption studies (Sandstrom 1985); NIH ODS fact sheet
scheduling_implication: Iron can reduce the absorption or effect of zinc. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: High-dose zinc can modestly reduce iron absorption through competition for shared intestinal transport; the effect is small at typical supplement doses.
scheduling_implication: Zinc can reduce the absorption or effect of iron. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: Iron and manganese share the DMT1 intestinal transporter; high iron intake reduces manganese absorption.
scheduling_implication: Iron can reduce the absorption or effect of manganese. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: Coffee taken with or up to 1 hour after a meal reduced non-heme iron absorption by roughly 40-70%; coffee taken 1 hour before the meal had no effect.
evidence_scope: human absorption study (Morck 1983); NIH ODS fact sheet
scheduling_implication: Coffee can reduce the absorption or effect of iron. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: Phytate (in whole grains, legumes, nuts and seeds) binds non-heme iron and can lower its absorption by 50% or more in a phytate-rich meal.
evidence_scope: NIH ODS fact sheet (iron); human absorption studies
scheduling_implication: Phytate can reduce the absorption or effect of iron. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: Milk calcium and casein reduce non-heme iron absorption when consumed in the same meal as an iron dose.
evidence_scope: NIH ODS fact sheet (iron); human absorption studies
scheduling_implication: Milk / dairy can reduce the absorption or effect of iron. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: Soy protein and its phytate reduce non-heme iron absorption from the same meal.
evidence_scope: human absorption study (Lynch 1994); NIH ODS fact sheet
scheduling_implication: Soy foods can reduce the absorption or effect of iron. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

from_mechanism_name: Antacid / gastric-pH-raising mineral salt (Ca carbonate, Mg/Al hydroxide, Na bicarbonate)
evidence_text: Antacids raise stomach pH and carbonate can complex iron, reducing non-heme iron absorption; iron is usually separated from antacids by about 2 hours.
evidence_scope: NIH ODS fact sheet (iron); drug-nutrient interaction references
scheduling_implication: Antacids can reduce the absorption or effect of iron. Take them at least 2 hours apart.

evidence_text: Adding phytase to phytate-rich meals breaks down phytate and increased non-heme iron absorption in human studies.
scheduling_implication: Taking phytase together with iron (within about 1 hour) can help iron work better.

evidence_text: Phytate binds zinc in the gut and is the main dietary inhibitor of zinc absorption; high-phytate meals can substantially lower zinc uptake.
scheduling_implication: Phytate can reduce the absorption or effect of zinc. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: Phytate binds calcium and modestly reduces calcium absorption from the same meal.
scheduling_implication: Phytate can reduce the absorption or effect of calcium. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: In a human study, large doses of beta-carotene taken together with lutein lowered lutein absorption; the two carotenoids compete for incorporation into micelles and chylomicrons.
scheduling_implication: Beta-carotene can reduce the absorption or effect of lutein. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: Lutein can likewise reduce beta-carotene absorption when both are taken together in large doses, through competition for micellar uptake.
scheduling_implication: Lutein can reduce the absorption or effect of beta-carotene. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: Plant sterol or stanol intake (about 2 g/day) lowers plasma beta-carotene by roughly 10-25% by displacing it from intestinal micelles.
scheduling_implication: Plant sterols can reduce the absorption or effect of beta-carotene. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: Plant sterol or stanol intake modestly lowers plasma lycopene by displacing it from intestinal micelles.
scheduling_implication: Plant sterols can reduce the absorption or effect of lycopene. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: Plant sterols displace carotenoids from intestinal micelles; other carotenoids in mixed blends are likely affected similarly, although data are mainly for beta-carotene and lycopene.
scheduling_implication: Plant sterols can reduce the absorption or effect of mixed carotenoids. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

from_mechanism_name: Lipid carrier / co-ingested dietary oil (fish, krill, MCT, seed oils)
evidence_text: Vitamin E is absorbed together with dietary fat; taking it with a fat-containing meal or oil improves absorption compared with a fat-free intake.
scheduling_implication: Take vitamin E with a fat-containing meal or together with dietary oils (fish/krill oil, MCT, seed oils) to improve its absorption.

from_mechanism_name: Lipid carrier / co-ingested dietary oil (fish, krill, MCT, seed oils)
evidence_text: Vitamin K1 is absorbed together with dietary fat; taking it with a fat-containing meal or oil improves absorption.
scheduling_implication: Take vitamin K1 with a fat-containing meal or together with dietary oils (fish/krill oil, MCT, seed oils) to improve its absorption.

from_mechanism_name: Lipid carrier / co-ingested dietary oil (fish, krill, MCT, seed oils)
evidence_text: Vitamin K2 (MK-4) is fat-soluble and is absorbed better with a fat-containing meal or oil.
scheduling_implication: Take vitamin K2 (MK-4) with a fat-containing meal or together with dietary oils (fish/krill oil, MCT, seed oils) to improve its absorption.

from_mechanism_name: Lipid carrier / co-ingested dietary oil (fish, krill, MCT, seed oils)
evidence_text: Vitamin K2 (MK-7) is fat-soluble and is absorbed better with a fat-containing meal or oil.
scheduling_implication: Take vitamin K2 (MK-7) with a fat-containing meal or together with dietary oils (fish/krill oil, MCT, seed oils) to improve its absorption.

from_mechanism_name: Lipid carrier / co-ingested dietary oil (fish, krill, MCT, seed oils)
evidence_text: Preformed vitamin A is fat-soluble; dietary fat supports its absorption, although absorption is fairly efficient even with little fat.
scheduling_implication: Take vitamin A (retinol) with a fat-containing meal or together with dietary oils (fish/krill oil, MCT, seed oils) to improve its absorption.

evidence_text: Piperine (5 mg/day) increased plasma CoQ10 levels compared with CoQ10 alone in a small human study.
scheduling_implication: Taking piperine together with CoQ10 (within about 1 hour) can help CoQ10 work better.

evidence_text: Piperine increased the plasma beta-carotene response to a beta-carotene supplement in a small human study.
scheduling_implication: Taking piperine together with beta-carotene (within about 1 hour) can help beta-carotene work better.

mechanism_type: catechin inhibition of folic acid uptake
evidence_text: Green tea extract reduced the bioavailability of a folic acid dose (peak level about 39% lower) in healthy volunteers.
scheduling_implication: Green tea can reduce the absorption or effect of folic acid. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

mechanism_type: tea polyphenol inhibition of folic acid uptake
evidence_text: Black tea reduced folic acid bioavailability less than green tea in the same volunteer study; evidence is limited.
scheduling_implication: Black tea can reduce the absorption or effect of folic acid. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: Citrate greatly increases aluminum absorption from aluminum hydroxide (several-fold in human studies); aluminum antacid labeling warns against combining it with citrate products, especially with reduced kidney function.
scheduling_implication: Avoid taking citrate products (e.g., calcium or magnesium citrate) together with aluminum antacids: citrate greatly increases aluminum absorption, which can build up and cause harm.

mechanism_type: high-dose zinc reducing calcium absorption at low calcium intake
evidence_text: Very high zinc intake (about 140 mg/day) reduced calcium absorption when calcium intake was low; no effect is expected at usual doses.
scheduling_implication: Zinc can reduce the absorption or effect of calcium. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: Calcium binds fluoride to form poorly soluble calcium fluoride; taking fluoride with milk or calcium supplements lowers fluoride absorption.
scheduling_implication: Calcium can reduce the absorption or effect of fluoride. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: Magnesium binds fluoride in the gut and reduces fluoride absorption when taken at the same time.
scheduling_implication: Magnesium can reduce the absorption or effect of fluoride. Take them at least 4 hours apart.

evidence_text: Aluminum-containing antacids bind fluoride in the gut and reduce fluoride absorption.
scheduling_implication: Aluminum antacids can reduce the absorption or effect of fluoride. Take them at least 4 hours apart.
